articles.title: Audit Logging in Phoenix Without Leaking Passwords
articles.excerpt: Audit Logging in Phoenix Without Leaking Passwords Why your Ecto audit log misses update_all, and other traps I found while building one. Sooner or later, every app gets the question: "Who changed thi…
articles.body: Audit Logging in Phoenix Without Leaking Passwords Why your Ecto audit log misses update_all , and other traps I found while building one. Sooner or later, every app gets the question: "Who changed this record, and when?" Sometimes it comes from a compliance checklist. More often it comes during an incident, when a customer's plan was downgraded, a price changed, or an admin account appeared from nowhere, and nobody can say how. I recently built audit logging for a Phoenix app. The first version took ten minutes. Finding everything that was wrong with it took a lot longer. This post walks through the traps I hit, how to avoid them in plain Ecto, and how PostgreSQL triggers cover the changes your Elixir code never sees.

articles.title: The 89% Short: why a hallucination rate needed a video to be honest
articles.excerpt: I published a new walkthrough yesterday: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/7swT71hR-A4 — and it exists because "89%" keeps getting quoted like a verdict when it's really a measurement with a very specifi…
articles.body: I published a new walkthrough yesterday: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/7swT71hR-A4 — and it exists because "89%" keeps getting quoted like a verdict when it's really a measurement with a very specific setup behind it. The reason I filmed it: I kept seeing the number passed around as proof that a model "makes things up constantly," and that framing breaks down the moment you look at the eval. So the Short walks through exactly what produced the 89% — the prompt set, the sampling, and the fact that the score counts confident fabrication, not hesitation or hedging. Two runs on slightly different seeds moved the number by several points, which is the part nobody tweets.

articles.body: Driving Claude Code through plan, code and QA by hand takes a lot of prompts. oh-my-claudecode (OMC) is a plugin that adds multi-agent orchestration on top: describe a feature once and let staged agents work through it. This is how the README sets it up, and what to check before you trust the result. Install it as a Claude Code plugin These are Claude Code slash commands. Enter them one at a time, because pasting both lines at once fails, as the README warns: /plugin marketplace add https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode Then: /plugin install oh-my-claudecode Run the setup command inside the session: /omc-setup If you prefer the npm CLI path instead of the marketplace flow, the README gives: npm i -g oh-my-claude-sisyphus@latest npm may print a prebuild-install deprecation warning…

articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have filtered out starlight from James Webb Space Telescope observations to see a giant exoplanet emerge in the darkness.
articles.body: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST.

articles.body: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image released Nov. 5, 2026, provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier , who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus. Read more about this group of stars and what scientists can learn from it. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G.
